did_you_know.text: The Hebrew word mishpatim is related to the root sh-p-t, meaning laws and judgments. The chapter presents practical rules immediately after Sinai, linking faith with everyday behavior.

The cycle of six years of service followed by freedom in the seventh echoes the patterns of the Sabbath and the sabbatical year. It sets a clear limit on servitude and prevents it from becoming permanent.
The mezuzah in this verse means a doorpost, not the scroll later known by that name. Piercing the ear was a public ritual marking the servant’s choice to remain in the household.

The female servant has a different status from the male servant: the following verses allow for her to marry her master or his son. Her sale is therefore connected with family arrangements, not only with manual labor.
From the words “food, clothing, and marital rights,” the rabbis derived basic obligations of a husband toward his wife. The verse became an important source for discussing rights within marriage.
The verse distinguishes intentional killing from an accidental death. This idea later developed into the cities of refuge, where someone who caused a death unintentionally could flee.

Shevet means compensation for the time the injured person cannot work, while “he shall surely be healed” includes medical expenses. The verse presents an early principle that an attacker is responsible for both financial loss and treatment.
The word pelilim is connected with legal proceedings and judges. Even when no one dies, the Torah does not leave the dispute to private revenge but directs it to an orderly judgment.
“An eye for an eye” became a symbol of proportional justice. However, the rabbis understood it as financial compensation for the injury, not as a command to blind the offender literally.
The law protects a servant’s body: permanently damaging an eye or tooth requires the servant’s release. In this way, it recognizes a right to freedom even in a society where servitude existed.

This verse presents the principle of negligence: the ox’s owner is held responsible because he knew the animal was dangerous and failed to restrain it. What the owner knew beforehand matters, not only the act itself.
An uncovered pit is treated as a hazard for which the person who dug it or left it open is responsible. It is an early example of the duty to prevent dangers in places where others may pass.
